newsitem.title: UK: EBRD predicts another solid year in 1997.
newsitem.headline: EBRD predicts another solid year in 1997.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) said on Wednesday this year was likely to be a repeat of the 1996 performance with further rises in income and costs kept under control.
The Bank reported a rise in operating profit to 97.3 million Ecu last year from 82.9 million in 1995, while net project disbursements increased 18 percent to 1.16 billion Ecu.
"We expect to show financial results (in 1997) to mirror last year's," EBRD vice president for finance, Bart le Blanc, told a news conference.
Banking operations now account for almost half of total income, compared to 36 percent in 1995, while costs were 10 percent below budget, he said.
A priority for the Bank will be to build up its reserves which currently stand at 8.2 percent of total outstanding disbursed loans and equity investments.
Net profit last year was 4.9 million Ecu, compared to 7.5 million in 1995, because of a larger provision for losses.
Le Blance said that as EBRD's investments increase in the less advanced members of the old East Bloc, so there is an increase in risk.
The Bank now has investment projects in all 26 member countries, with its first projects signed for Tajikistan and Bosnia.
Its total portfolio of loans and equity investments now stands at 7.7 billion Ecu.

EBRD President Jacques de Larosiere said the bank would stick to its priorities of concentrating on the private sector, collaborating with local financial institutions, increasing equity investments and diversifying within the region in which it operates.
He noted there had been a slight pause in equity investments last year, which dipped to 15 percent of the year's commitments from 16 percent the previous year.
"We would like to be more active. But it is not always very easy to be able to take equity participation," he added.
Even though the Bank is moving further eastwards in the region, there remained plenty of scope in the more successful economies of central Europe, such as infrastructure projects, de Larosiere said.
